body:
My thanks to Scott for digging this up for me.  I'm putting it up almost
unchanged, but I should point out that Shadow had some interesting feedback
on the commune movement.  My take on the sites that I looked at in
conjunction with her post was that many of them were religious communities,
but there are instances - one she cited on the Atlantic seaboard, more or
less, and the Hog Farm up in Oregon for two - that are longstanding and
currently self-sustaining communes.  

In article <l99802l0l30l00.IAAl3242@ladder02.news.aol.com>
rossgl2345@aol.com (RossGl2345) writes:

[In regard to a discussion of the Bible generally and specifically as a
rationale for some acts, like bombing clinics.]

>We agree on the bible. (Even scrapie agrees with us;
>he was just adopting someone else���s argument).

This may sting.  I agree that using the Bible as a rationale for bombing
abortion clinics is loony.  I also agree that the Bible does not
recognize fetuses as humans - and in fact, it recognizes the death of a
fetus as a form of property damage, not of murder.

Ex. 21:22-25 is often very incompletely read by many of the those who
enjoy quoting it.

"If, when men come to blows, they hurt a woman who is pregnant and she
suffers a miscarriage, though she does not die of it, the man
responsible must pay the compensation demanded of him by the woman���s
master;  he shall hand it over, after arbitration.  But should she die,
you shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for
hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stroke for stroke."
(the Jerusalem Bible, Reader���s Edition)

However, I do *not* agree with the contention that the Bible is at best
only as much worth considering as is the Manifesto, or the problems
drawn attention to by the Manifesto.  The argument "oh, well  the Bible
got written a long time ago" evades several things:  there are instances
- nowhere near 100%, but certainly instances - where events mentioned in
the Bible refer to things which actually happened.

We know, for instance, that the New Testament does in fact refer to
Roman functionaries actually serving, from other sources.  We know that
there were Temples built in Jerusalem - we can verify this from the
results of the archeology adjacent to the site.  Many of the migrations
of peoples as discussed in the Old Testament did in fact occur;  the
Bible may well be <ahem> elaborating considerably in its depictions of
their motives and their actions, but it remains the sole source for
descriptions of some of those.

Much of what Kaczynski argues in the Manifesto cannot be objectively
shown to be true, valid or useful.  We���ve seen it recently to be
subjectively true - Shadow experiences it as truth in her life, while
Paul Cox experiences it as false.  From a subjective point of view, the
Bible can���t just be dismissed out of hand as easily as some here would
- it has, after all, lots of subscribers.  It���s also a very important
thing in cultural history and mythology - far more so, I think even
Shadow���d agree - than the Manifesto.

>"The bomber is merely mean and small.  He had no
>ideas of consequence, killed at random, had no followers
>and reshaped nothing." - a quote from Gelernter

Here, I respectfully disagree with Gelernter;  TK had ideas of
consequence  - those he���d borrowed wholesale from others.  What he
failed to do was to meaningfully articulate any extension forward from
them.  He didn't have a plan;  he had an obsession which rationalized
his behavior within the confines of his own head.

What is original with TK in the manifesto is, well, not nearly as good
as what he cribbed.

I���ve been mumbling about doing this for a bit, so I might as well put up
or shut up.  Here are some notes I made on the Manifesto recently;  for
almost all of them, you will want to have a copy of the Manifesto to
hand, as I���m criticizing passages which jumped out at me but not quoting
them at length.  What I don���t do properly, because I found it boring and
very unpersuasive, is really go through the "power process" argument he
makes.  If someone would like to go through it thoroughly while
defending it, that���s fine - it might stimulate me to make the
counterargument. (Me?  Argue?  Never, eh?)

Para 21:  Conflicts with P 20:  hostility of leftists versus their
alleged masochism.  More importantly, P 21 rather misses the long period
of time when economic justice was demanded forcefully but with
considerable grace and tact by MLK and others.

Para 29:  Where does this line of reasoning extend to?  TK seems to be
arguing that the scholastic and economic inequalities which were
maintained for hundreds of years in the US between whites and blacks are
somehow essential to the maintenance of blackness.

What would he say to a Paul Robeson?  (For those of you who don���t know:
Princeton football star and Cum Laude grad in the 20���s;  law school
grad, Rhodes Scholar, playwright and actor, who ultimately relocated to
the USSR in disgust over the racial divide in the US.  His son, Paul
Robeson Jr., has a lot of very interesting things to say about the
multiple schools of thought in American black intellectual history, and
about how disappointing it is to see the media demanding that there be
*one* black school of thought in much of its coverage.)

The discussion of the "power process" - how much of this is accurate
sociology, and how much of this is TK projecting what *he* felt about being
distanced from the Noble Savage by Society onto everyone?

Para 61:  How much of this discussion of mere obedience at work can be
read in light of what we now know about TK working at a job much like
the one he���s describing here but *working for his brother,* and being
essentially ordered by his brother to stop treating one of his coworkers
bizarrely?

Para 69:  TK should���ve tried visiting Africa before praising the
"stoicness" in the face of the risk of disease.  While there is
stoicness in the face of AIDS *in particular* that stoicness is couched,
in the African writing I���ve read, in a very high degree of bitterness
about the West only developing a concern for disease in Africa when that
disease poses a threat to the West.  I can���t remember the quote exactly,
but on hearing about projections about the spread of disease, one Kenyan
responded "So, we may have many people dying of AIDS.  There are already
many ways to die here" with a clear sense of astonishment that only one
disease was of interest to his interviewer.  (Of course, that disease
happened to be one of the few the interviewer couldn't be easily cured of
on their return home, should they have the misfortune to contract it...)

Indeed, one of the Buddhist sutras is the story of a woman who visits
the Buddha, distraught over the loss of one of her children.  Can the
Buddha resurrect her child?  The Buddha will, but first she must travel
until she meets a family untouched by such a tragedy.  She spends a year
traveling the countryside, and of course discovers that she cannot find
such a family.  When she returns to the Buddha, she���s understood that
all families are struck, and all grieve.  She still grieves;  only
Buddha was able to be nonattached - it is a condition which comes with
being Enlightened, not from the ordinary experience of disease and
death. (And remember, this sutra was first doing its important religious
work ca. 2000 years ago, and in a part of the world where our leaders
would like us to believe that "life is valued less than it is here."
Apparently not, since this is an important enough sutra to have survived
the span of time.)

Para 73:  Communes have been attempted periodically to escape the
pressures outlined in this paragraph.  Almost without exception, they���ve
failed within a span of a very few years.  (And those communities which
have succeeded in maintaining their identity base their rejection of
society less on such mundane topics as who works for whom and why than
they do on a deeply-held religious faith.)

Para 74:  His discussion of why modern societies��� birthrates fall versus
those of primitive societies is very incomplete.  In countries where
there is still a considerable amount of low-cash, subsistence, "power
process" lifestyle the birthrate has over the past two decades begun to
fall precipitously.  (Growth rates which were 7%/year in much of Latin
America and Asia have fallen to below 3%/year - still unsustainably
high, in all likelihood, but they continue to fall.)  The main common
denominator here is literacy.  Not algebra, not advertisements for
Gilette razors, but governments��� being able to at least educate a
substantial part of the populace to the level where it can read.

Now, TK might well make Caliban���s argument from the Tempest on behalf of
those forced to abandon their "essence" by learning to read:

CALIBAN:  You taught me language; and my profit on���t Is, I know how to
curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!

However, I haven���t heard that there are a lot of aboriginal activists out
campaigning to stop the spread of literacy in the third world. There may be
- I just haven���t heard about them.

Para 75:  This is simply piss-poor anthropology.  The hunters in
hunter-gatherer societies are indeed the men;  however, in most of the
cultures where it���s been looked at carefully, the vast bulk of the food
the people eat comes from the work of women, boring drudgery harvesting
and preparing the vegetables they���ve gathered.  One famous example is an
Amazonian tribe which subsists largely on manioc root.  Collecting a
root vegetable is tiring, backbreaking work - and it���s the work of
women.  Raw manioc is poisonous - it must be extensively cooked to leach
out the poisons.  Guess who���s in charge of the cooking?

This parenthetical is particularly entertaining:  "In young women the
process is more complex, with greater emphasis on social power; we won���t
discuss that here."  Read before we knew who the author was, that phrase
doesn���t have quite the connotation of a dodge that it does now that we
know more about his skills relating to women, directly or as sisters in
law.

Para 84:  "a surrogate activity that is directed toward an artificial
goal that the individual pursues for the sake of the fulfillment that
he gets from pursuing the goal, not because he needs to attain the goal
itself."

This is another great instance of projection, and it requires that we
accept his earlier assertions about the artificiality of goals he
doesn���t himself approve of.

It���s also interesting, to me at least, to contrast this with the
considerable body of thought, most clearly defined for me in Buddhist
teachings but present also in some Jewish and Christian teachings, about
the utility of recognizing that attaining goals, ultimately, is never
necessary - it���s the act of pursuing them, and the state of mind you���re
in while pursuing them, which distinguishes you.

TK rejects that line of reasoning - and is in fact making a false
consciousness argument about it.  (To be fair, he���s actually not saying
anything about state of mind when pursuing what he sees as legitimate
"power process" goals.)

Para 87:  The Motives of Scientists.  I found this section to be
particularly weak.  I think that again, because of his isolation even
when he was in an academic setting, he didn���t give sufficient weight to
the notion that there are people who really are just curious, and get a
great deal of satisfaction from engaging that curiosity.

For instance, the two best-read science publications are probably Nature
and Science magazines.  Most of the people I know who read them spend as
much or more time looking over the survey articles at the front of the
magazine on topics wholly unrelated to their own research as they do on the
one or two papers in an issue which may be directly relevant to their work.
For instance, I find the current debates over the mass and rate of
expansion of the universe, and the question of whether it will eventually
be able to reverse its rate of expansion and collapse in on itself
incredibly interesting.  I don���t have the background to read the research
on the topic, so I read the surveys for a general readership instead.

One of the things I value most about working in a setting where there
are people around who���ve read the same reviews is just bullshitting
about them.

So when TK asserts:  "Is the chemist curious about the appropriate
classification of a new species of beetle? No," he may well be wrong.
If the classification of the species of beetle is written carefully
about and the relevance of that assignment is made clear, it may well be
engaging to lots of people.  Stephen Gould has made a tidy living from
explaining the relationships of extinct snails, his specialty, to the
general public, for goodness��� sake!  (Of course, he's also gone farther
afield.)

Para 88:  A long discussion of why Mr. Teller is a Bad Man.  Which is
fine.  But when we think of physicists, most of us think of Einstein
before Teller, and Einstein is an exemplar of someone who completely
contradicts this statement - but by no means the only one.

Also, I expect TK would suggest that examining the abundance of lead
isotopes to study the age of the solar system is of no conceivable
interest to anyone.  Yet the scientist who started that work at Caltech
in the early 60���s ultimately forced the oil companies and car companies
to give up on using leaded gasoline because of the public health threat
posed by lead settling from tailpipes.  It���s sort of surprising to see
someone with so much formal training who doesn���t appreciate the odd
turns which research can take.

Para 89:        The last sentence is a criticism of scientists��� motives.
However, those motives are just fine - exactly as TK states them - with
a number of systems of belief:  being here, now, as Leary would
encourage us - not focusing on the goal (as TK would urge us to) but on
the journey.

Para 92:  ���This is interesting;  he essentially denies moral agency to
scientists.  A letter published this week in Nature from a group of
people working on the Convention on Biological Diversity points out
"Whether or not this protocol will provide for the consideration of
social and economic issues is as yet undecided."  This point is made
critically - the authors of the letter are imploring the larger
community of scientists to make that consideration an *explicit* goal
because they recognize that as it now stands, it is an *implicit* goal
and they are required to consider it but not voice their considerations.

They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social implications"
explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being given an ethical
agency, and that they need to be able to act on it in the open.

In talking with people who I think have worked in what are to me
genuinely negative fields of research - weapons design at Lawrence
Livermore, for instance - I find that those who are directing and
actively engaged in the work are there because they think they are doing
the right thing for the country, even with all the risks their work
entails, and that by doing the right thing for the country, they do the
right thing for the world.  These people are actively aware of and
engaging their moral agency - in a direction which I choose not to.

The people who seem unwilling to do so are bright people who act more in
support than in directing the work.  They see employment in the field as
ethically neutral, as just a legal job, and don���t like thinking about
the costs and benefits of the work.

Para 96:  Concludes with:  "In order to get our message before the
public with some chance of making a lasting impression, we���ve had to
kill people."  I wonder if TK realizes the extent to which he���s not made
a lasting impression, but has simply become another media commodity
-even in the hands of some of his supporters   Unapack sends a copy of
the Manifesto out with every order of Unabomber goods they sell through
their site - but I wonder how many of the buyers are pitching it and
using the stickers merely for their admittedly quite good Situationist
humor value?

-Peter
